lines.text: You walk up to the school gate, and the new guard holds up a hand.
Teachers use the back entrance, sir.
You're seventeen. Your body is thirty-one.
There's grey in your hair, your knees click on the stairs, and your phone just buzzed with your weekly screen time report.
Ten hours a day. Up twelve percent.
So what if every hour on your phone aged you one day?
Not your battery. Not your eyes. Your whole body. One hour on a screen, one day older.
And it only counts the screen in your own hands. Remember that. It matters later.
Let's go back to where it started. Your sixteenth birthday.
That night you scroll in bed until three in the morning. Five hours. Dance videos, memes, a man pressure-washing a driveway.
In the morning, the number floating over your head says sixteen years and five days.
You figure it's a glitch. Then you spend the weekend gaming with your best friend Kai. Twenty hours.
Monday, you have stubble. Real stubble. At sixteen.
Kai is on his phone just as much as you, and Kai still looks twelve.
So you test it. Kai holds your phone and reads every message out loud. The number doesn't move.
Rule one: one hour on a screen, one day on your body. Rule two: only the screen in your hands counts.
Now the math. American teenagers average about eight and a half hours of screen entertainment a day.
That's eight and a half days of aging, every single day. Almost nine years for every year you live.
At your pace, you graduate at thirty-six. By twenty-one, you'd get the senior discount.
And honestly? The first few months are kind of great.
Nobody asks for your ID at the movies. The bank calls you sir. A waiter hands your mom the kids' menu and hands you the wine list.
But your body is keeping score.
At seventeen, your back hurts when you sneeze. You make a noise every time you stand up. You say back in my day about last Tuesday.
And the phone keeps calling you back. A typical teen gets around two hundred and thirty notifications a day.
Two hundred and thirty little taps on the shoulder. Each one says, just one minute. It is never one minute.
You try to quit. Day one, your hand keeps reaching for a phone that isn't there.
Your pocket buzzes, and nothing is in it. In one study, eighty-nine percent of college students said they felt phantom vibrations like that.
Day two, you find your old handheld console, just to check the battery. Four hours. Four days.
So you make Kai your human phone. He reads your messages, scrolls your feed, and narrates your videos.
Okay, a cat falls off a table. Now it's angry. Now it's... eating?
It works for about two weeks.
Then Kai gets tired of being your phone. And you get tired of hearing the whole internet in Kai's voice.
The group chat moves on without you. Plans get made at midnight, and you find out at noon.
Nora invites everyone to the lake. Everyone except the guy who looks like a substitute teacher.
At seventeen and a half, you're thirty-one. The mirror is the worst app you own.
So you get on a bus to the one person in your family who never owned a smartphone. Grandma Rosa.
Grandma Rosa lives two hours out of town, with a garden, a chess board, and a phone that flips.
She looks at your grey hair, doesn't ask a single question, and hands you a shovel.
Here's what science says happened to the rest of us. Psychologist Gloria Mark measured how long people focus on one screen before switching.
Around two thousand four, it was about two and a half minutes. Today, it's about forty-seven seconds.
At Grandma's house, there's nothing to switch to. So you dig. You cook. You lose at chess. Eleven times.
And somewhere in week two, you notice it. The number over your head hasn't moved in nine days.
That night, by the fire, Grandma tells you why she never bought a smartphone.
In nineteen seventy-two, she says, every hour of television made her one day older.
She isn't seventy-nine. She's sixty-one.
It runs in the family. She switched off the only screen she had, and never looked back.
Those days don't come back, she says. But the ones you live with your eyes up are the only ones that feel long.
Then winter comes. One Saturday, Grandma walks up the ridge trail to fix a fence, the way she has for forty years.
At four o'clock, a storm rolls in. At five, she isn't back. Her flip phone goes straight to voicemail.
The rescue team is two hours away. The trail splits into six paths, and the snow is erasing her footprints.
There's one thing that can find her. A screen. A map, her last signal, the weather radar.
You don't care about the days it will cost. The problem is your hands. You need them for the flashlight, the rope, and her.
And then you remember rule two. Only the screen in your hands counts.
You call Kai. It's been a month. He answers anyway.
Kai becomes your eyes. He watches the radar from his room and talks you up the mountain, turn by turn.
Left at the broken pine. Two hundred steps. Her phone last pinged near the creek.
Your knees are thirty-one and they're screaming. But your eyes are up, and you see what a screen would never show you. One red glove in the snow.
She's under a rock ledge, ankle twisted, absolutely furious at the fence.
You carry her down. Kai guides the rescue team to the trailhead. Nobody looks at a single number all night.
In the morning, the number over your head says thirty-one years and two days. Two days for that trip. Worth it.
Here's the real part. Your phone can't age your face.
But the average American spends around four and a half hours a day on their phone.
From age ten to eighty, that's about thirteen years of your life. Awake. Looking down.
Nobody gives those years back. You just get to choose what the next ones look like.
So you keep the phone. You just stop letting it hold you.
On Monday, you walk up to the school gate. The guard holds up a hand.
Teachers use the back entrance, sir.
You grin. Not today. Today I've got a class to catch up on.
So tell me. What did your screen time say yesterday? Be honest. And yes, you're watching this on a phone.
Subscribe. It takes one second. That's not even a day.
